title: Korean Fish Cake Soup
subtitle: Eomuk broth with skewered fish cakes and radish
excerpt: Flat fish cake sheets are sliced into strips, threaded onto skewers if desired, and simmered in a clean anchovy and radish broth with garlic and a touch of gochugaru. This recipe serves 4 and takes 30 minutes. It is one of the most recognisable street foods in Korea and a simple, warming home soup in equal measure.
sourceNotes: Eomuk guk, also called odeng guk, has been eaten in Korea since fish cakes were introduced from Japan during the early twentieth century. On Korean streets, fish cakes on skewers sit in large pots of broth that pedestrians can pull out and eat for a small fee, drinking the broth from small cups. It is considered the definitive Korean winter street food and appears equally often as a home-cooked soup.

glossaryTerms.definition: Eomuk is the Korean word for fish cake, a processed seafood product made from ground white fish mixed with starch and seasonings, then formed into flat sheets or tubes and boiled or fried. Korean eomuk has a springy, slightly dense texture and a mild savoury flavour. It absorbs surrounding broth easily during cooking. Eomuk is sold in flat rectangular sheets in Asian supermarkets, usually in the freezer section.

Odeng guk is another common name for Korean fish cake soup, where 'odeng' is the Koreanised pronunciation of the Japanese word 'oden' and 'guk' means soup. The terms eomuk guk and odeng guk are used interchangeably in Korea. On the street, the fish cakes are usually threaded onto long skewers standing upright in a large pot of simmering broth; at home they are more often served cut into pieces in a bowl.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes around 30 minutes. The broth is the central element: it should taste clean, lightly savoury and slightly smoky from the dried anchovies. The
itself is mild and absorbs the broth during cooking, which is why a good stock makes a significant difference to the finished soup. This home version of
skips the street-food skewers in favour of a straightforward bowl.

Korean fish cakes from the freezer section need to be thawed before cooking. Rinse them briefly under warm water and pat dry. If the fish cakes are very flat, fold them into accordion shapes or cut them into strips before adding to the broth. Do not overcook them: 5 to 7 minutes in simmering broth is enough.

content.text: Make the anchovy stock. Place the dried anchovies in a large saucepan with the water and the radish pieces. Bring to the boil and simmer for 15 minutes. Remove and discard the anchovies.
Add the garlic, soy sauce and gochugaru to the stock. Stir to combine.
Add the fish cake strips to the simmering broth. Cook for 5 to 7 minutes until the fish cakes are heated through and have absorbed some of the broth flavour.
Add the spring onions in the final 2 minutes. Taste the broth and adjust with salt if needed.
Ladle the soup into deep bowls, making sure each portion gets a good amount of fish cake, radish and broth. Serve immediately alongside rice or on its own.

items.symptom: Fish cakes are rubbery and tough after cooking
items.cause: They were overcooked, or they were not fully thawed before going into the broth
items.fix: Thaw the fish cakes completely and rinse before adding to the soup. Simmer them gently for no more than 7 minutes. They should be springy and soft, not chewy.

items.symptom: Broth tastes flat and does not have enough depth
items.cause: The anchovies were not simmered long enough, or too few were used
items.fix: Simmer the anchovies for a full 15 minutes rather than a shorter time. Taste the stock before adding anything else. If it still tastes weak, add a small piece of dried kelp (dashima) and simmer for a further 5 minutes.

items.symptom: Radish is still hard and raw-tasting
items.cause: The radish was cut too thick or not added early enough
items.fix: Add the radish at the same time as the anchovies and cook it through the full 15-minute stock stage. Cut the pieces no more than 5mm thick.

content.text: Korean fish cake soup is the smell of Korean winters. Street stalls in Seoul, Busan and across the country keep large iron pots of it simmering all day, and people stop to pull out a skewer and warm their hands around a cup of broth between errands. At home it is a fast, easy soup that does not require much planning. The fish cakes are sold ready to cook and the stock is simple to make from scratch in 15 minutes. It is the kind of dish that feeds people quickly and makes them feel looked after.
